Mini RFC 4000: The Test Protocol




Bernstein                Standards Track


Status of this Memo

   This memo defines a synthetic miniature RFC used by the chunker test
   suite.  It exercises headers, footers, front matter, a table of
   contents, numbered sections, an ABNF grammar block, a table, and the
   service-part tail.  Distribution is unlimited.

Abstract

   This document defines the FOO method for the Test Protocol used to
   validate offline text chunking without network or model access.

1 Introduction

   The Test Protocol carries fictional signaling between two synthetic
   endpoints.  This introduction exists so that the cleaner has a
   realistic body-start anchor after the front matter blocks.

   It also provides enough surrounding prose that chunk boundaries fall
   between paragraphs rather than inside them.

1.1 Scope

   This miniature document covers only the FOO method.  This section is
   deliberately short so that it merges into a neighboring chunk per
   the minimum-size rule.

2 The Foo Method

   The FOO method carries application level information along the
   signaling path of an established dialog.  It never changes the
   dialog state itself and it never affects the session description.

   A FOO request may be sent inside an early dialog or a confirmed
   dialog.  The recipient answers it with a final response and the
   transaction finishes without any effect on the media streams.

   Senders of FOO requests include an Allow header listing FOO in
   every request they emit.  Recipients that do not understand the
   method answer with a 501 response as the base specification says.

   Full Copyright Statement

   The example block above quotes a boilerplate heading from the
   middle of the document.  It must not trigger the service tail cut
   because the tail cut only considers the last quarter of pages.

   The FOO method reuses the transaction machinery of the base
   protocol.  Proxies forward FOO requests statelessly and they never
   need to inspect the body of the request at all.

%%PAGE%%
RFC 4000                    The Test Protocol                June 2002

   The grammar of the method is specified below in ABNF.  The rule
   must never be split across two chunks because parsers need it as a
   unit.  The rule text is intentionally surrounded by enough prose
   that whichever way the paragraphs pack, the grammar lines share a
   chunk with at least one full paragraph on each side of the block.

      Foo =  ( "FOO" / "f" ) HCOLON foo-param
             / "BAR"
             ; the foo-param follows the HTTP rules

   The table below lists the header fields of the method.  It must
   stay atomic as well because column readers scan it as one block.

   Header field          where       proxy
   Foo                   R           opt
   Bar                   R           opt

   Implementations that support the extension report it in a
   Supported header.  Implementations that do not support it simply
   ignore FOO requests and answer them with a final rejection code.

   Implementations that support the extension also advertise it in a
   Allow header listing the method.  The method is midpoint safe and
   it may be issued by either side of the dialog at any time.

   Proxies that receive a FOO request for an unknown dialog target
   forward it along the route set without inspecting it.  This keeps
   the method compatible with stateless intermediate elements and it
   avoids any need for midpoint transaction state to be allocated.

   Endpoints should rate limit FOO requests to avoid flooding their
   peer with application payloads.  A sender that exceeds the peer's
   declared capacity receives a congestion signal and must back off.

2.1 Request Body of Foo

   The body of a FOO request carries a plain text payload whose media
   type is text/foo.  The payload is opaque to the protocol itself.

   Bodies larger than a single transport frame are fragmented by the
   layer below and reassembled before delivery to the application.

Appendix A Test Appendices

   This appendix collects the auxiliary material of the specification.
   It lists the known implementation quirks reported by early
   implementers and it explains how the conformance suite exercises
   each of them in isolation before the interop events.

Appendix A.1 Collecting Details

   The collection procedure starts with a plain text transcript of the
   signaling exchange.  The transcript is annotated with the detected
   quirks, and every annotation refers to the section of the base
   specification that defines the expected behavior for the exchange.

4 Acknowledgments

   The working group members listed in the discussion archive
   provided extensive review of earlier versions of this document.
